author: ali-ahmad

fields.name: watts
fields.label: Load
fields.hint: Total watts the cable will carry, from the appliance labels or the home load calculator.

fields.name: length_m
fields.label: Cable run
fields.hint: One-way length from the distribution board to the load, following the walls.

fields.name: volts
fields.label: Voltage
fields.hint: Required for DC: enter the battery or system voltage. On AC leave it blank for the standard single or three-phase voltage.

fields.name: inverter_eff
fields.label: Inverter efficiency (DC)
fields.hint: DC only: for a battery-to-inverter cable the watts are what the inverter delivers, and the battery also supplies its loss, so current = watts ÷ (efficiency × volts). Enter 1 for a DC load wired straight to the battery. Enter the bank's nominal voltage above: the calculator works at the battery's low-battery cut-off voltage, where the current is highest.

fields.name: load_type
fields.label: Type of load
fields.hint: Motors, compressors and ACs get a breaker with a margin because they run near full current for long periods.

fields.name: ambient_c
fields.label: Air temperature around the cable
fields.hint: Hottest air the cable sits in: a conduit under a sunny roof or in a hot wall gets far hotter than the room. The default is a Pakistani summer value; every cable rating is reduced for it.

fields.name: circuits
fields.label: Circuits in the same conduit
fields.hint: How many circuits share this conduit or bundle. Cables packed together heat each other, so each one carries less.

fields.name: pf
fields.label: Power factor
fields.hint: Leave blank to use the load type: {{d.pf_by_load_type.inverter_compressor|1}} for an inverter AC, {{d.pf_by_load_type.compressor|1}} for a non-inverter compressor, {{d.pf_mixed|1}} for mixed loads and motors. Heaters are 1.0; enter it for them. Ignored for DC.

fields.name: margin
fields.label: Safety margin
fields.hint: The cable is rated for the design current times this margin.

answer: A {{in.watts|int}} W single-phase load over a {{in.length_m|int}} m run in conduit needs a {{out.area_mm2|1}} mm² copper cable ({{out.pk_size|raw}} in Pakistani sizes), rated {{out.ampacity_a|int}} A, on a {{out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB, with a {{out.drop_pct|1}}% voltage drop. The cable must carry the design current of {{out.ib_a|1}} A times a {{out.margin|2}} safety margin and keep the drop under {{out.limit_pct|int}}%.
how: Design current = {{out.watts}} W ÷ ({{out.k|2}} × {{out.current_v|2}} V × {{out.pf|2}} power factor × {{out.inverter_eff|2}}) = {{out.ib_a|1}} A (the first factor is one for single phase and DC, root three for three phase; the last is the inverter efficiency on a DC battery feed, one on AC; on DC the voltage is the battery's at its low-battery cut-off, where the current is highest). MCB (or DC fuse above the largest MCB) = next standard size above {{out.breaker_design_a|1}} A = {{out.breaker_a|int}} A. The cable must be rated at least {{out.min_cable_a|1}} A, the larger of {{out.ib_a|1}} A × {{out.margin|2}} and the MCB, and be at least {{out.min_mm2|1}} mm² for this circuit type: {{out.area_mm2|1}} mm² ({{out.pk_size|raw}}) is rated {{out.ampacity_a|int}} A. Voltage drop over the {{in.length_m}} m run = {{out.drop_v|1}} V, which is {{out.drop_pct|1}}% of {{out.volts}} V, within the {{out.limit_pct|int}}% limit.
key_facts: Wire size = the smallest copper cable whose current rating covers the design current × {{d.margin|2}} (and the MCB) and whose voltage drop over the run stays under {{d.vdrop_limit_other_pct|int}}% for power circuits or {{d.vdrop_limit_lighting_pct|int}}% for lighting.

Pakistani wire sizes are strands/diameter: 7/29 is rated as a {{out.area_mm2|1}} mm² cable and carries {{out.ampacity_a|int}} A in conduit; 7/36 as {{ex.4.out.area_mm2|1}} mm² at {{ex.4.out.ampacity_a|int}} A (IEC 60364-5-52, PVC copper, in conduit, corrected for {{out.ambient_c|int}} °C air).

A {{in.watts|int}} W load at {{out.volts|int}} V draws {{out.ib_a|1}} A and fits on 7/29 with a {{out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB; a {{ex.0.in.watts|int}} W load draws {{ex.0.out.ib_a|1}} A and needs {{ex.0.out.area_mm2|1}} mm² ({{ex.0.out.pk_size|raw}}) with a {{ex.0.out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB.

Long runs are sized by voltage drop, not current: {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W over {{ex.1.in.length_m|int}} m needs {{ex.1.out.area_mm2|1}} mm² although {{ex.1.out.ampacity_only_mm2|1}} mm² would carry the current.

formula.text: I_b = P ÷ (k × V × PF); I_n = next standard ≥ I_b; I_z = I_z,table × f_temp × f_group ≥ max(I_b × margin, I_n); ΔV% = k_v × L × I_b × ρ ÷ A ÷ V × 100
lines: I_b = design current; k = 1 for single phase and DC, √3 for three phase
I_n = MCB rating; I_z = cable current rating for the installation method
f_temp, f_group = IEC 60364-5-52 correction factors for the air temperature and the circuits in one conduit; three phase uses the three-conductor ratings
k_v = 2 for single phase and DC (there and back), √3 for three phase
L = one-way run in metres; ρ = resistivity of copper; A = cable area in mm²
Minimum sizes: lighting circuits and power circuits each have a floor whatever the current

sections.h2: How does this wire gauge and cable size calculator pick a size?
p: It works the way an electrician does, in three steps. First the design current: watts ÷ (volts × power factor), or ÷ (root three × volts × power factor) on three phase. Second the MCB: the next standard size above the design current, with a {{out.margin|2}} margin first for motors, compressors and ACs. Third the cable: the smallest copper size whose rating for the installation method covers the design current × {{out.margin|2}} and the MCB, and whose voltage drop over your run stays under the limit.

For the default {{in.watts|int}} W at {{in.length_m|int}} m that is {{out.ib_a|1}} A, a {{out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB and a {{out.area_mm2|1}} mm² cable ({{out.pk_size|raw}}) rated {{out.ampacity_a|int}} A, with a {{out.drop_pct|1}}% drop. The MCB is always rated at or below the cable, so the breaker protects the cable.

sections.h2: What is the 7/29 wire ampere rating (2.5 mm² wire amps)?
p: 7/29 copper wire is rated as a {{out.area_mm2|1}} mm² cable here and carries {{out.ampacity_a|int}} A in conduit inside a wall in {{out.ambient_c|int}} °C air ({{out.ampacity_30c_a|int}} A in the IEC table at {{data.cables.derating.ambient_factors.4.0|int}} °C), a little more when clipped on the surface. With the {{out.margin|2}} safety margin that means a design current of about {{out.ib_a|1}} A, the default {{in.watts|int}} W load, fits on 7/29 with a {{out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB and room to spare ({{out.min_cable_a|1}} A needed against {{out.ampacity_a|int}} A).

A {{ex.4.in.watts|int}} W load on the same supply draws {{ex.4.out.ib_a|1}} A and needs a cable rated {{ex.4.out.min_cable_a|1}} A, above what 7/29 can carry, so the calculator moves to {{ex.4.out.pk_size|raw}} ({{ex.4.out.area_mm2|1}} mm²), rated {{ex.4.out.ampacity_a|int}} A, with a {{ex.4.out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB. 7/29 is also the minimum size for any socket or AC circuit.

sections.h2: How many amps can 4 mm² wire carry?
p: {{ex.4.out.area_mm2|1}} mm² copper, sold as 7/36 in Pakistan, carries {{ex.4.out.ampacity_a|int}} A in conduit in {{ex.4.out.ambient_c|int}} °C air. It is the usual choice for a kitchen socket ring, a geyser plus sockets, or an AC on a long run. In the example below a {{ex.4.in.watts|int}} W load at {{ex.4.in.length_m|int}} m gets 7/36 with a {{ex.4.out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB and a {{ex.4.out.drop_pct|1}}% drop. Above that the calculator moves to 7/44.

sections.h2: What is copper wire ampacity and why does the installation method matter?
p: Ampacity is the current a cable can carry continuously without its insulation getting too hot. The ratings here are for PVC-insulated copper from IEC 60364-5-52: method B1 is a cable in conduit inside a wall, which is most Pakistani house wiring and traps heat, so it is rated lower than method C, a cable clipped to a surface in free air. Pick the method that matches your installation.

Heat and grouping reduce the rating further. The IEC table is for {{data.cables.derating.ambient_factors.4.0|int}} °C air; the calculator multiplies every rating by the IEC correction factors for the air temperature you enter (in {{out.ambient_c|int}} °C air a PVC cable keeps {{out.ambient_factor|2}} of its rating) and for the circuits sharing the conduit. The default air temperature is a cautious Pakistani summer value awaiting review by a PEC-registered engineer. Aluminium is not rated here.

sections.h2: Is there a cable size chart for Pakistani wire sizes?
p: The table below is one: common single-phase loads at {{in.length_m|int}} m with the mm² size, the Pakistani name, the current rating, the MCB and the voltage drop. The names count the strands and their diameter in thousandths of an inch: 3/29 is three strands and is rated as 1 mm² for lighting points, 7/29 is seven strands rated as 2.5 mm² for sockets and ACs, 7/36 as 4 mm², 7/44 as 6 mm². Bigger sizes are rated by their real area: {{data.cables.pk_sizes.4.name|raw}} is {{data.cables.pk_sizes.4.area_mm2|2}} mm², just under {{data.cables.cables.5.area_mm2|int}}, so it is rated as {{data.cables.pk_sizes.4.rated_as_mm2|int}} mm²; {{data.cables.pk_sizes.5.name|raw}} ({{data.cables.pk_sizes.5.area_mm2|2}} mm²) as {{data.cables.pk_sizes.5.rated_as_mm2|int}} mm² and {{data.cables.pk_sizes.6.name|raw}} as {{data.cables.pk_sizes.6.rated_as_mm2|int}} mm² for main feeds.

A 7/29 is actually a little larger than 2.5 mm², but it is rated as 2.5 mm² here to stay on the safe side. Always buy cable with the size printed on the sheath from a known maker; thin or copper-clad wire sold as 7/29 does not carry 7/29 current.

sections.h2: What wire size for a 5 kW load?
p: On single phase at {{ex.0.out.volts|int}} V a {{ex.0.in.watts|int}} W mixed load draws {{ex.0.out.ib_a|1}} A, so it needs a {{ex.0.out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB and a {{ex.0.out.area_mm2|1}} mm² cable ({{ex.0.out.pk_size|raw}}) rated {{ex.0.out.ampacity_a|int}} A, with a {{ex.0.out.drop_pct|1}}% drop over {{ex.0.in.length_m|int}} m. This is the size of a typical main feed for a small home or a sub-main to a floor. The same five kW on three phase splits over three live wires and needs a smaller cable.

mistakes: Sizing the cable to the load alone. The cable must also be rated above the MCB that protects it, otherwise the breaker lets the cable overheat before it trips.
Measuring the run across the room. Cable follows walls, ceilings and the distribution board, so the real run and the voltage drop are longer than the straight line.
Ignoring voltage drop on long runs. A cable that carries the current comfortably can still lose too much voltage over {{ex.1.in.length_m|int}} m; motors and compressors suffer most.
Treating copper-clad or aluminium wire as copper. Both need a larger size and different terminals; the ratings here are for copper only.
Trusting the name on the roll. A cheap 7/29 with thin strands is not 2.5 mm²; buy from a known maker with the size printed on the sheath.
safety: These sizes are planning values for copper cable in {{out.ambient_c|int}} °C air with {{out.circuits|int}} circuit in the conduit; the air temperature default awaits review by a PEC-registered engineer. A licensed electrician must confirm the cable, MCB and earth on site.

faq.q: Does this wire size calculator use Pakistani wire sizes?
faq.a: Yes. Every result shows the mm² size and the Pakistani name (3/29, 7/29, 7/36, 7/44 and up), using the copper current ratings of IEC 60364-5-52 for cable in conduit or clipped on a surface.

faq.q: What is the maximum load on 7/29 wire?
faq.a: 7/29 carries {{out.ampacity_a|int}} A in conduit in {{out.ambient_c|int}} °C air. With the {{out.margin|2}} planning margin a {{in.watts|int}} W single-phase load ({{out.ib_a|1}} A) fits with a {{out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB; a {{ex.4.in.watts|int}} W load ({{ex.4.out.ib_a|1}} A) does not and moves up to 7/36.

faq.q: What size wire for a five kW load at {{out.volts|int}} V?
faq.a: {{ex.0.out.area_mm2|1}} mm² copper ({{ex.0.out.pk_size|raw}}) with a {{ex.0.out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB: the load draws {{ex.0.out.ib_a|1}} A and the cable is rated {{ex.0.out.ampacity_a|int}} A.

faq.q: Which wire for a {{ex.0.in.watts|int}} W load on a {{ex.0.out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB?
faq.a: {{ex.0.out.area_mm2|1}} mm² ({{ex.0.out.pk_size|raw}}), rated {{ex.0.out.ampacity_a|int}} A in conduit in {{ex.0.out.ambient_c|int}} °C air. The cable must cover both the MCB and the design current × {{ex.0.out.margin|2}} ({{ex.0.out.min_cable_a|1}} A here, which is what decides it), so that the breaker always protects the cable.

faq.q: Does cable length change the wire size?
faq.a: Yes, through voltage drop. {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W at {{ex.1.in.length_m|int}} m needs {{ex.1.out.area_mm2|1}} mm² to keep the drop at {{ex.1.out.drop_pct|1}}%, under the {{ex.1.out.limit_pct|int}}% limit, while the same load at {{in.length_m|int}} m fits on {{out.area_mm2|1}} mm².

faq.q: What cable for a three-phase motor?
faq.a: The current divides over three phases: a ten kW motor at {{ex.2.out.volts|int}} V draws {{ex.2.out.ib_a|1}} A per phase and takes a {{ex.2.out.breaker_a|int}} A MCB on {{ex.2.out.area_mm2|1}} mm² ({{ex.2.out.pk_size|raw}}) cable.

faq.q: Which wire between the battery and the inverter?
faq.a: DC current is high because the voltage is low: {{ex.3.out.watts|int}} W from a {{ex.3.out.volts|int}} V battery is {{ex.3.out.ib_a|1}} A by the time the battery is low, needing {{ex.3.out.area_mm2|1}} mm² ({{ex.3.out.pk_size|raw}}) over a {{ex.3.in.length_m|int}} m run with a DC-rated breaker or fuse. Keep battery cables as short as possible.

The number of copper strands and each strand's diameter in thousandths of an inch: 7/29 is seven strands of twenty-nine thousandths of an inch. The calculator converts each to its area in mm² and rates it as the largest IEC size that area reaches, so a cable is never rated above its real copper.
